base64_cases.description: Standard base64 (RFC 4648 section 4, with padding). Protocol rule: decode strictly (reject URL-safe alphabet, embedded whitespace, wrong padding). Python b64decode(validate=True) and Swift Data(base64Encoded:) both validated at generation time on the Python side.

cases.reference: w023 fixed test public key (65-byte uncompressed point)

cases.note: URL-safe alphabet '-' is outside the standard alphabet
URL-safe alphabet '_' is outside the standard alphabet
Whitespace inside the string must be rejected by strict decoding
'!' is not part of any base64 alphabet

MIME folded base64 (embedded LF) must be rejected by strict decoding

public_key_cases.description: Protocol v1.x public key wire format: base64 of the 65-byte SEC1 uncompressed point. Format check on BOTH ends: length must be 65 AND first byte must be 0x04, BEFORE any curve math. Compressed points, SPKI/PKCS#8 DER and PEM containers are known encoding variants of the same key and MUST be rejected.

valid.format: SEC1 uncompressed point 0x04 || x || y (65 bytes)

known_variants.note: SEC1 compressed point (0x02/0x03 || x, 33 bytes). A valid curve point, but the v1.x protocol accepts ONLY the uncompressed form. Backend _decode_public_key rejects it (length != 65); Swift P256 x963Representation also rejects it.

X.509 SubjectPublicKeyInfo (PKCS#8 public key envelope), DER-encoded. Same key material, different container. The v1.x protocol does not accept SPKI: it is rejected by the 65-byte/0x04 format check. Recorded for future protocol evolution only.

PEM armor of the same SPKI key ('-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----'). A text container, not the protocol wire format. Rejected by base64 strict decode (embedded newlines) and by the length check. Recorded for reference only.

reject_cases.note: 64 bytes: raw x||y without the 0x04 prefix
66 bytes: right length + one trailing byte
65 bytes but prefix 0x05 (invalid point form)
33 bytes SEC1 compressed form with 0x03 prefix
Empty value
Not valid base64 at all

der_cases.description: DER-encoded ECDSA signatures (RFC 3279). Structure check before crypto: SEQUENCE tag 0x30, declared length matches, exactly two INTEGERs, no trailing data. NOTE (review finding): the current production checker does NOT enforce INTEGER minimality/padding (see der-r6) and does NOT enforce low-s. Recorded as-is; tightening is proposed in docs/crosslang-serialization-proposal.md, not implemented here.

reject_cases.note: 0x31 (SET) instead of 0x30 (SEQUENCE)
Truncated below the 8-byte minimum
Two extra bytes appended after the SEQUENCE
SEQUENCE containing only one INTEGER (missing s)
Declared SEQUENCE length is one byte shorter than actual data

Same (r,s) as the official RFC 6979 'sample' signature but r encoded WITHOUT the required leading 0x00 (non-minimal BER). Empirical production behaviors recorded above exactly as measured. RFC 3279 strict DER would reject this encoding.

payload_contract.description: EXACT signed payload byte contract. The signature covers precisely these bytes - nothing more, nothing less. Both ends must be able to rebuild them deterministically from the manifest fields.
rules: P2: first line is the domain separator ('WorkCam-Sig-v1.1' or 'WorkCam-Sig-v1' depending on the version field)
P3: then one line per field in the fixed order: version, record_id, sequence_number, previous_record_hash, photo_hash, capture_timestamp, device_reported_time, device_id, location
P4: every line is 'key=value' with a single '=' separator
P5: null field values serialize as the literal token 'none' (previous_record_hash, location); a present location serializes as 'lat,lon,accuracy,altitude' with altitude 'none' when null
P6: line separator is a single 0x0a (LF); CR (0x0d) is never emitted; field values must not contain LF or CR
P7: the payload ends with exactly one trailing LF
P8: the signature/public_key fields are NOT part of the payload

unicode_cases.description: Unicode cases: the protocol signs UTF-8 BYTES. NFC vs NFD vs bidi controls produce different bytes and therefore different signatures - both are valid, neither may be normalized. Swift rule: use String.utf8 (or Array(string.utf8)); never precomposedStringWith*. Python rule: str.encode('utf-8'); never unicodedata.normalize on the verification path.

cases.note: NFC precomposed LATIN SMALL LETTER E WITH ACUTE (2 UTF-8 bytes)
NFD decomposed 'e' + U+0301 COMBINING ACUTE (3 UTF-8 bytes). Same visible glyph as u2, DIFFERENT bytes, therefore different signature. Never auto-normalize on either side.
Contains U+200F RIGHT-TO-LEFT MARK (zero-width bidi control). Allowed by the protocol (not a newline) and signed as-is.
Astral plane character U+1F309 (4-byte UTF-8 unit)
Combining mark + superscript two; multi-script mix
Empty string: 0 bytes; sha256 equals the FIPS empty-input KAT

newline_cases.description: Newline discipline: payload lines are ALWAYS 0x0a (LF) only, including a final trailing LF. Any CR/LF variant rebuild must fail signature verification. Field values containing LF or CR are rejected by structure validation before crypto.

reject_cases.note: Same logical lines joined with CRLF. Swift-side trap: must fail.
Same logical lines joined with bare CR. Must fail.
Payload without the final 0x0a. Must fail.
Payload with an extra final newline. Must fail.

float_cases.description: Float serialization rules. v1.1 is the normative cross-language rule (10-significant-digit %.10g with integer detection and guaranteed decimal point); v1.0 uses Python repr semantics and is the known cross-language hazard (see proposal). The v1.1 rule must be ported VERBATIM to Swift - a bare String(format: "%.10g") is NOT sufficient (integer branch and '-0.0' handling differ). See W023CrosslangVectorTests.swift formatFloatV11() for the port.

v1_0_repr_risk_table.note: v1.0 embeds floats with Python str()/repr() shortest-round-trip formatting. Swift String(describing:) is NOT guaranteed byte-equal for these (exponent thresholds differ between the two runtimes) - this is the documented v1.0 drift risk. Swift output for the same bits: PENDING_MAC_VERIFICATION.

rules: R1: only finite values (NaN/Infinity rejected before formatting)
R2: if the value is an integer value (value == int(value)) and not negative zero, emit the integer digits followed by '.0'
R3: otherwise emit %.10g (10 significant digits); if the result has neither '.' nor an exponent, append '.0'
R5: values with exponent < -4 render in exponential form ('1e-05', '1.5e-07')

null_absent_cases.description: null vs absent equivalence: JSON null, key-absent and (for location/altitude) empty inner values all serialize to 'none' in the canonical payload and are INTERCHANGEABLE. A signature made from the null form verifies under the absent form and vice versa. Swift rule: model these fields as optionals and decode with decodeIfPresent (JSONDecoder maps both null and absent to nil). The empty-string trap ('' serializes to 'key=' not 'key=none') is NOT equivalent and is rejected by structure validation.

equivalence_case.note: Both JSON forms MUST rebuild the same payload bytes and the same verification result.

empty_string_trap.production_error_sample: previous_record_hash must be 64 hex characters when present

iso8601_cases.description: ISO 8601 rules. CRITICAL cross-language rule: the timestamp inside the canonical payload is an OPAQUE STRING - never parse-then-reformat it. 'Z' and '+00:00' denote the same instant but are different bytes with different signatures. The production validator is a SHAPE regex, not a calendar: e.g. 2026-13-01T00:00:00Z passes the shape check (documented finding; tightening proposed in the proposal doc, not implemented here).

shape_only_accepted_example.finding: month 13 passes the shape regex; the production validator does not check calendar semantics

timezone_cases.description: Timezone offsets: three textual representations of the SAME UTC instant. Each has different bytes and therefore a different signature. A verifier that normalizes timestamps (e.g. Swift ISO8601DateFormatter parse then re-format) will rebuild different payload bytes and break verification. Rule: compare and sign the literal string.
timezone_cases.rule: bytes_in_payload_are_the_contract: capture_timestamp and device_reported_time are signed as opaque strings

field_order_cases.description: Field order: the canonical payload uses a FIXED field order (see fixed_order below), independent of the JSON key order of the incoming manifest. Both ends MUST rebuild lines in this exact order - never rely on dictionary/JSONEncoder ordering. This case is signed once; a verifier loading the shuffled-order JSON must rebuild identical payload bytes and the signature must verify.
field_order_cases.canonical_json_note: If/when the protocol ever signs JSON directly, use RFC 8785 (JCS) canonicalization - proposed in docs/crosslang-serialization-proposal.md, NOT part of v1.x.

tamper_cases.description: Tamper cases: every modification of one byte (payload, signature, base64 layer, DER layer, domain separator, timezone digit) must cause verification failure. Both implementations must reject every case in this list.

reject_cases.note: single byte flipped inside the domain separator line
first byte of photo_hash value flipped
final 0x0a flipped to 0x0b
'1.1' -> '0.1' single-byte change in the version line
latitude 39.9042 -> 39.9043 (one decimal digit)
timezone offset +00:00 -> +01:00 (same clock reading, different offset)
domain line v1.1 -> v1.0 while version field still says 1.1
last DER byte flipped; may still parse as DER but verification must fail
8 bytes removed from the end
two zero bytes appended
valid DER with r and s exchanged (structural check passes, crypto must fail)
final base64 character replaced (payload bytes may or may not change)
structurally valid DER signature produced by a DIFFERENT P-256 key over the same payload

version_cases.description: Protocol version compatibility. The version field value is BOUND to the domain separator line. Unknown versions are rejected by structure validation. REVIEW FINDING (recorded as-is, not changed here): the production canonical_payload silently falls back to the v1.0 domain separator for any version string outside {'1.0','1.1'}; a Swift port MUST NOT copy this fallback - it must reject unknown versions before serialization (the structural check does reject the manifest first, so the fallback is unreachable through the public API, but it is still a divergence trap for fresh implementations).

unknown_version_behavior.cross_lang_rule: Both ends MUST check version in {'1.0','1.1'} BEFORE building the payload and MUST reject otherwise. Do not reproduce the Python fallback domain separator.

negative_cases: t04-version-field-flip (version line byte change breaks signature)
